1.title: Scrum Values and the Agile Manifesto
1.text: Welcome to Module 2: Scrum Values and the Agile Manifesto. Module 1 gave you the theory. This module covers the behaviors that make the theory work, and the mindset that Scrum reflects. Two lists to learn, and one skill: matching each Manifesto idea to the Scrum feature that carries it.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. List the five Scrum values and say what each means. Explain what the values do for a Scrum Team. Tell values from pillars. State the Manifesto's four values and twelve principles. Match Manifesto ideas to the Scrum features that reflect them. And spot the traps: false values, the idea that only the left side counts, and the mistake of treating the Manifesto as Scrum.

1.title: Case Check-In: One More Feature
1.text: A scene from RideLoop. It is day four of Sprint eight, and Grace Whitfield asks Maya for one more small feature this Sprint. Maya is tempted to say yes, just to keep the peace. The Developers worry that the Sprint Goal is now at risk. You are the Scrum Master, and you ask yourself which value the team needs most. Hold that thought; by the end of the next few slides you will know.

1.title: The Five Scrum Values
1.text: The five Scrum values are commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage. A simple memory aid: commit, focus, be open, respect, have courage. Say them to yourself a couple of times now, because answer lists can include impostors, and you want to spot the wrong ones at a glance. The diagram adds where you see each value in practice; those examples are exam practice, not Guide text.

1.title: What Each Value Means
1.text: What does each value mean? Commitment: the team commits to its goals and supports each other. Focus: attention goes to the work of the Sprint, for the best progress toward the goals. Openness: honesty with stakeholders about the work and its difficulties. Respect: members regard each other as capable, independent people. Courage: doing the right thing and tackling tough problems. And remember the impostors: trust, transparency, collaboration, discipline and accountability are not on the list.

1.title: What the Values Do
1.text: What do the values do? They steer the team's work, actions and behavior. Every decision, and how the team applies Scrum, should reinforce the values and never weaken them. Team members learn the values by working with the events and artifacts. And when people live them, the three pillars come to life and trust grows. In a scenario question, choose the answer that strengthens a value, and reject the one that hides bad news, accepts every request, or splits attention.

1.title: Where Each Value Shows Up
1.text: Where do you see each value in action? This slide goes beyond the Guide, but it helps with scenarios. Commitment shows in the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done. Focus shows in the Sprint Goal and the Daily Scrum. Openness shows in visible artifacts and honest events. Respect shows when the team plans together and honors the Product Owner's decisions. Courage shows when someone says an item will not fit, or refuses to call unfinished work Done. And it answers the RideLoop question from the start of the module. Maya needs courage to say no, or to negotiate, when Grace asks for one more feature in the middle of the Sprint.

1.title: Values and Pillars
1.text: Values and pillars are different lists. The pillars, transparency, inspection and adaptation, make the process empirical. The values, commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage, describe how people behave. They work together. Without openness there is no real transparency, because people hide problems. Without courage the team does not adapt when inspection shows an uncomfortable truth. So never add transparency to the list of values.

1.title: The Agile Manifesto
1.text: Now the Agile Manifesto. It was written more than twenty years ago by seventeen practitioners, among them Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, the creators of Scrum. It has four values and twelve principles, and it is a mindset, not a framework. Notice that the Scrum Guide never mentions it. The learning objectives do, which is why the exam can ask about it. The diagram shows the four value pairs, each with the left side valued more than the right, and the twelve principles behind them.

1.title: The Four Values and Scrum
1.text: The Manifesto values the left side more than the right. Individuals and interactions over processes and tools: Scrum has a self-managing team guided by few rules. Working software over comprehensive documentation: every Sprint produces a usable Increment that meets the Definition of Done. Customer collaboration over contract negotiation: stakeholders join the Sprint Review, and the Product Owner keeps the Product Backlog ordered. Responding to change over following a plan: the Product Backlog is emergent, and the events exist to inspect and adapt. The right side still has value. The Guide never mentions the Manifesto, so this matching goes beyond it.

1.title: Principles 1 to 6 and Scrum
1.text: Principles one to six, the first half of the twelve. The Guide does not mention them, so this matching goes beyond it. Early and continuous delivery: an Increment every Sprint. Welcome changing requirements: the Product Backlog can be reordered. Deliver frequently: Sprints of one month or less. Business people and developers work together daily: stakeholders collaborate, and the team refines and plans together. Motivated individuals, trusted: a self-managing, empowered team. Face-to-face conversation: events bring people together at the same time and place.

1.title: Principles 7 to 12 and Scrum
1.text: Principles seven to twelve, the second half. Again, this matching goes beyond the Guide. Working software measures progress: a usable Increment, and the Definition of Done. Sustainable pace: Sprints at a pace the team can keep. Technical excellence and good design: quality built in through the Definition of Done. Simplicity, the art of maximizing the work not done: lean thinking and an ordered Product Backlog. Self-organizing teams: the Developers decide how. Regular reflection: the Sprint Retrospective. You do not need the exact wording; you need the matches.

1.title: Manifesto and Scrum Compared
1.text: Do not confuse the two. The Manifesto is a mindset of four values and twelve principles, and it answers the question: why work this way? Scrum is a framework with accountabilities, events and artifacts, and it answers the question: how, inside a few rules? The Manifesto prescribes no events and no roles. And if an option says Scrum is aligned with the Manifesto simply because it is agile, that answer is circular. Name the feature.

1.title: Traps: What the Exam Expects
1.text: Here are the traps. Values and pillars are separate lists. Respect means treating people as capable, independent people. The Manifesto prefers the left side, but the right side still has value. The Manifesto is not Scrum. Keep the counts apart: four values and twelve principles for the Manifesto, five values and three pillars for Scrum. And overtime to hit a plan goes against a sustainable pace. In scenarios, reject answers that hide problems, dodge hard truths, scatter attention, blame people, or drop the team's goals.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. The values are commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage. They direct the team and make the pillars real. The Manifesto has four values and twelve principles, and it is a mindset. For alignment questions, match an idea to a specific Scrum feature. Left over right does not mean the right side is worthless. And the Manifesto has no roles or events; Scrum does. Now test yourself.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. On day three of Sprint nine, Wei finds that an item is much harder than expected, but the team is proud of its record and nobody wants to say so. Which Scrum value should the Scrum Master help the team practice most? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B, openness. Sharing the problem early lets the Developers adapt the plan and talk scope with the Product Owner. Keeping the plan at any cost, or working harder, hides the problem.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A RideLoop manager says the Manifesto prefers working software over comprehensive documentation, so the team should stop documenting anything. What is the best reply? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. The Manifesto values the left side more, but the right side keeps its value. Scrum does not prescribe documentation either way. The Definition of Done decides what the product needs.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. The RideLoop Developers work evenings in the last days of every Sprint to finish everything they planned. Which Manifesto principle and Guide idea does this go against? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A, a sustainable pace. The Guide links a sustainable pace in Sprints to better focus and consistency. Overtime to hit a plan is not sustainable.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which list names the five Scrum values? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B: commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage. Transparency is a pillar, and trust and discipline are not Scrum values.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which pairing of a Manifesto idea with the Scrum feature that reflects it is correct? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. Self-organizing teams match a self-managing Scrum Team. Responding to change matches the emergent Product Backlog, working software matches the Increment, and frequent delivery matches short Sprints.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: B, openness. Question two: D, the right-hand items keep their value. Question three: A, a sustainable pace. Question four: B, commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage. Question five: D, self-organizing teams match a self-managing Scrum Team. That completes Module 2. Next, Module 3 covers the Scrum Team and the Developers.
